name: Medulla oblongata
func: The lowest part of the brainstem, joining the brain to the spinal cord. It runs life-support reflexes like breathing rhythm, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting, and it is where most motor fibers cross sides.

levels.kid:
The **medulla** is the very bottom of your brain, where it turns into the long cord that runs down your back.

It is like the brain's **autopilot**. It keeps you **breathing** and keeps your **heart** beating all day and all night, even while you sleep, without you ever having to remember.

It also helps you **swallow** your food, **cough** when something tickles your throat, and **sneeze**.

Here is a cool fact: the messages that move your right hand start on the left side of your brain. They switch sides right in the medulla, like two roads crossing in an X.
levels.hs:
The **medulla oblongata** is the lowest part of the **brainstem**. It is about 3 cm long and runs from the **pons** above to the **spinal cord** below, which it joins at the **foramen magnum**, the big hole in the base of the skull. Behind it sits the **cerebellum**, and the lower half of the **fourth ventricle** lies on its back surface.

On the front you can see two ridges called the **pyramids**, made of motor fibers from the cortex. At the bottom, most of these fibers cross to the other side: the **decussation of the pyramids**. That is why each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. Beside each pyramid is an oval bump, the **olive**.

The medulla houses vital **cardiovascular** and **respiratory centers** that set breathing rhythm and adjust heart rate and blood pressure. It controls reflexes like **swallowing**, **coughing**, **gagging**, **sneezing** and **vomiting**.

Cranial nerves **IX** (glossopharyngeal), **X** (vagus), **XI** (accessory) and **XII** (hypoglossal) leave from the medulla. Because it runs the body's basic life support, serious damage here can be fatal.
levels.college:
The medulla is split into a **closed (caudal)** part, which contains the central canal, and an **open (rostral)** part, where the canal widens into the fourth ventricle.

Key internal structures:
- **Pyramids**: corticospinal fibers; about 85–90% cross in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
- **Dorsal column nuclei** (gracile and cuneate): second-order neurons for fine touch and proprioception. Their axons cross as **internal arcuate fibers** and ascend as the **medial lemniscus**.
- **Inferior olivary nucleus**: sends **climbing fibers** to the cerebellum through the **inferior cerebellar peduncle**.
- **Nucleus ambiguus**: motor to the pharynx and larynx (via IX and X).
- **Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus**: parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs and gut.
- **Nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS)**: receives taste and visceral sensation, including signals from **baroreceptors** and **chemoreceptors**.
- **Hypoglossal nucleus**: tongue muscles, under the hypoglossal trigone.
- **Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract**: pain and temperature from the face.
- **Area postrema**: a chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting, outside the blood–brain barrier.

Blood comes from the **vertebral arteries**, the **anterior spinal artery** (medial medulla) and the **posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)** (lateral medulla).
levels.phd:
Breathing rhythm is generated in the **ventral respiratory column**. The **pre-Bötzinger complex** (Smith and Feldman, 1991) is the kernel for inspiratory rhythm: its glutamatergic neurons, including those derived from **Dbx1** progenitors, fire in synchronized bursts using persistent sodium and calcium-activated nonselective cation currents, while network synchronization is the primary driver. The **retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN)**, marked by **Phox2b**, senses CO2 and pH (via TASK-2 and GPR4) and drives breathing; PHOX2B mutations cause **congenital central hypoventilation syndrome**, in which breathing fails during sleep. A separate oscillator, the **parafacial respiratory group**, drives active expiration.

Blood pressure regulation runs through the **baroreflex**: stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch signal to the **NTS**, which excites the **caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM)**; GABAergic CVLM neurons inhibit the **rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM)**, the main sympathetic premotor drive to spinal preganglionic neurons. At the same time, the NTS drives vagal output from the **nucleus ambiguus** to slow the heart.

The **area postrema** detects circulating emetic agents, helped by fenestrated capillaries, and projects to the NTS and a distributed "vomiting central pattern generator" rather than a single anatomical center. The **raphe nuclei** of the medulla (raphe magnus, pallidus, obscurus) supply serotonin to the spinal cord, tuning pain transmission, motor excitability and thermoregulation.

The **inferior olive** neurons are electrically coupled by **connexin-36** gap junctions and show subthreshold oscillations, which may provide timing signals for cerebellar learning.
levels.expert:
Two classic medullary stroke syndromes are tested constantly:

- **Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**, from **vertebral artery** or **PICA** occlusion: vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, **dysphagia** and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral **Horner syndrome** (descending sympathetics), ipsilateral facial and contralateral body **pain and temperature loss** (crossed sensory loss), and ipsilateral limb ataxia. Strength is spared. **Vertebral artery dissection** after neck trauma is a key cause in young people.
- **Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome**, from **anterior spinal** or vertebral branch occlusion: contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid), contralateral loss of vibration and position sense (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral **tongue deviation** toward the lesion (hypoglossal).

**Tonsillar herniation** through the foramen magnum compresses the medulla, causing respiratory arrest; the **Cushing triad** (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) warns of raised intracranial pressure. **Chiari I malformation** (tonsils more than about 5 mm below the foramen magnum) causes occipital headache made worse by coughing and can be associated with a **syrinx**; **posterior fossa decompression** is the standard operation.

**Bulbar palsy** (lower motor neuron, as in ALS) gives a wasted, fasciculating tongue and nasal speech, while **pseudobulbar palsy** (upper motor neuron) gives a stiff tongue, brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability. **Brain death** testing focuses on medullary function: absent cough and gag reflexes and an **apnea test** with no breathing effort despite rising CO2.

**Hemangioblastomas** of the medulla occur in **von Hippel–Lindau disease**; **ependymomas** of the fourth ventricle are common in children.

keyPoints: Lowest brainstem segment, joins the spinal cord at the foramen magnum
Pyramidal decussation: why each brain half controls the opposite body side
Vital centers: breathing (pre-Bötzinger complex), heart rate, blood pressure
Cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII; reflexes like swallowing, cough and vomiting

test.q: Most corticospinal fibers cross the midline in the:
test.explain: About 85–90% cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla.

test.q: The small cluster of medullary neurons that generates inspiratory rhythm is the pre-______ complex.
test.explain: The pre-Bötzinger complex is the kernel of breathing rhythm.

test.q: Hoarseness, crossed pain/temperature loss and ipsilateral Horner syndrome point to occlusion of the:
test.explain: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, from PICA or vertebral artery occlusion.

test.q: In medial medullary syndrome, the tongue deviates:
test.explain: The paralyzed genioglossus on the lesion side cannot push, so the tongue points toward the weak side.

test.q: The vomiting trigger zone outside the blood–brain barrier is the area ______.
test.explain: The area postrema senses blood-borne emetic signals and relays to the NTS.
